Impose censorship on the national press.
Improve the relationship between the Government of India and the Indian States.
answerOptions.rationale: The Butler Committee, also known as the Indian States Committee, was appointed in 1927 with the specific objective of investigating and clarifying the relationship between the Paramount Power (the British Crown) and the Indian Princely States, and to make recommendations for the more satisfactory adjustment of the economic and financial relations between British India and the States. Its primary aim was indeed to improve the relationship between the Government of India and the Indian States, particularly to prevent disaffection among the rulers regarding their position vis-à-vis the British.

questions.question: Consider the following pairs:1. Radhakanta Deb : First President of the British Indian Association2. Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty : Founder of the Madras Mahajana Sabha3. Surendranath Banerjee : Founder of the Indian AssociationWhich of the above pairs is/are correctly matched?

answerOptions.rationale: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Radhakanta Deb was the first President of the British Indian Association, which was founded in Calcutta in 1851.Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty was a prominent figure and one of the founders of the Madras Native Association (established in 1852). The Madras Mahajana Sabha was founded much later, in 1884, by M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subrahmanyam Aiyar, and P. Anandacharlu.Pair 3 is correctly matched. Surendranath Banerjee, along with Anandamohan Bose, founded the Indian Association in Calcutta in 1876. It was one of the most important pre-Congress nationalist organizations.

questions.question: Who among the following was/were associated with the introduction of Ryotwari Settlement in India during the British Rule?1. Lord Cornwallis2. Alexander Read3. Thomas MunroSelect the correct answer using the code given below:

answerOptions.rationale: The Ryotwari Settlement system of land revenue was primarily introduced in parts of Southern India. Lord Cornwallis (1) is associated with the Permanent Settlement in Bengal. Alexander Read (2) and Thomas Munro (3) were the key figures associated with the introduction and implementation of the Ryotwari System, first on an experimental basis in the Baramahal region (Tamil Nadu) by Read in 1792, and later expanded significantly by Munro in Madras Presidency in the early 19th century. Under this system, revenue was collected directly from the cultivators (ryots).

questions.question: Consider the following statements:1. The Factories Act, 1881 was passed with a view to fix the wages of industrial workers and to allow the workers to form trade unions.2. N. M. Lokhande was a pioneer in organizing the labor movement in British India.Which of the above statements is/are correct?

answerOptions.rationale: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Factories Act of 1881, the first such legislation in British India, was primarily aimed at regulating the working conditions of child labor (prohibiting employment of children below 7, limiting working hours for those between 7 and 12, etc.) and providing some safety measures for factory workers. It did not address the issue of fixing wages or explicitly grant workers the right to form trade unions; those concerns came much later. Statement 2 is correct. Narayan Meghaji Lokhande is widely regarded as a pioneer of the labor movement in India. He began his work in Bombay, campaigning for better working conditions, reduced working hours, and weekly holidays for factory laborers in the late 19th century, well before formal trade unions emerged.

questions.question: The 'Swadeshi' and 'Boycott' were adopted as methods of struggle for the first time during the

answerOptions.text: agitation against the Partition of Bengal
answerOptions.rationale: The Swadeshi and Boycott movements were first adopted as methods of political struggle during the agitation against the Partition of Bengal in 1905. The Swadeshi movement called for the use of Indian-made goods, while the boycott movement urged the rejection of British-made goods and institutions. These methods were seen as potent tools to put economic pressure on the British government and foster Indian self-reliance.

answerOptions.text: visit of the Simon Commission to India

questions.question: Satya Shodhak Samaj organized

answerOptions.text: a movement for upliftment of tribals in Bihar

answerOptions.rationale: The Satya Shodhak Samaj (Truth-Seekers' Society) was founded by Jyotirao Phule in Maharashtra in 1873. Its primary objective was to work for the upliftment of the lower castes, particularly the 'untouchables', and women. It was a significant anti-caste movement that challenged Brahmanical dominance and advocated for social equality and access to education for all. Its focus was clearly an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra.

questions.question: The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals were related to

answerOptions.rationale: The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals, published in 1918, formed the basis of the Government of India Act, 1919. These proposals primarily aimed at constitutional reforms, introducing 'Dyarchy' in the provinces, expanding the legislative councils, and increasing Indian representation. They were a response to the growing demand for self-government in India and constituted a significant step in the process of constitutional development under British rule.

questions.question: What was the main reason for the split in the Indian National Congress at Surat in 1907?

answerOptions.text: Introduction of communalism into Indian politics by Lord Minto
Extremists' lack of faith in the capacity of the moderates to negotiate with the British Government
answerOptions.rationale: The Surat Split of 1907 was primarily caused by the ideological differences and growing distrust between the moderate and extremist factions within the Indian National Congress. The Extremists, led by leaders like Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Bipin Chandra Pal, had lost faith in the Moderates' constitutional methods of petitioning and negotiation with the British. They advocated for more assertive methods like Swadeshi, Boycott, and passive resistance to achieve Swaraj, which the Moderates largely opposed. Disagreements over the presidential candidate for the Surat session and the wording of key resolutions also exacerbated the conflict, leading to the formal split.

answerOptions.text: Aurobindo Ghosh's inability to be elected as the President of the Indian National Congress

questions.question: The plan of Sir Stafford Cripps envisaged that after the Second World War

answerOptions.text: India should be granted complete independence
India should be partitioned into two before granting independence
India should be made a republic with the condition that she will join the Commonwealth
India should be given Dominion status
answerOptions.rationale: The Cripps Mission of 1942 proposed that, after the conclusion of the Second World War, India would be granted Dominion status. This meant India would have internal autonomy but would still be nominally associated with the British Crown and the Commonwealth. The proposals also included the formation of an Indian Constituent Assembly to frame a new constitution, with provisions for provinces to opt out if they did not wish to join the Indian Union. Complete independence was not offered, nor was partition mandated at this stage.

questions.question: Which of the following acts designated the Governor-General of Bengal as the Governor-General of India?

answerOptions.rationale: The Charter Act of 1833 was a significant step towards the centralization of administration in British India. It made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India, thereby establishing a single authority over the entire British Indian territory. Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India.

questions.question: Which among the following was a primary reason for the economic ruin of Indian handicrafts during the first half of the 19th century?

answerOptions.text: High demand for Indian goods in Britain

answerOptions.rationale: The Industrial Revolution in Britain led to the mass production of goods, particularly textiles, at much lower costs than handmade Indian products. The British then imported these cheap machine-made goods into India, often at negligible duties, while Indian handicrafts faced high tariffs in Britain. This unequal competition, combined with the loss of patronage from native rulers, severely undermined and eventually ruined India's once-flourishing handicraft industries during the first half of the 19th century.

questions.question: The 'Vital-Vidhvansak', a pioneering journal for the untouchable people, was edited by:

answerOptions.rationale: Gopal Baba Walangkar (1840-1919) is credited with being one of the earliest social reformers to directly address the issues of untouchables in India. He started the monthly journal 'Vital-Vidhvansak' in 1888, specifically focusing on the upliftment and rights of the untouchable communities, making him a crucial figure in the early Dalit movement.

questions.question: Which of the following groups of plants, native to the Americas, were introduced to the Old World by European traders?

answerOptions.rationale: Potato, maize (corn), and tomato are all crops that originated in the Americas (the 'New World') and were introduced to Europe, Asia, and Africa (the 'Old World') after the Columbian Exchange, initiated by European explorers. These introductions had a profound impact on global agriculture and diets.

questions.question: The Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act (SPT Act) was a direct consequence of which major uprising?

answerOptions.rationale: The Santhal Uprising of 1855-56 was a violent rebellion by the Santhal people against the exploitation by zamindars, moneylenders, and the British administration. In response to the uprising and to prevent future unrest, the British government created the 'Santhal Paraganas' as a separate district and enacted laws (like the SPT Act) that made it illegal for Santhals to transfer land to non-Santhals, thereby protecting their land rights and traditional practices.

questions.question: In 1920, the All India Home Rule League changed its name to:

answerOptions.rationale: Under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, who became its president in 1920, the All India Home Rule League decided to change its name to 'Swarajya Sabha'. This change reflected the evolving political landscape and the Congress's adoption of 'Swaraj' (complete self-rule) as its primary goal, moving beyond the demand for mere Home Rule within the British Empire.

questions.question: Which of the following events occurred after the establishment of the Arya Samaj (1875)?

answerOptions.text: Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to clear ICS (1863)

answerOptions.rationale: To identify the event that occurred after the establishment of Arya Samaj (1875), we check the dates: 'Neeldarpan' was written in 1860, Satyendranath Tagore cleared ICS in 1863. Both are before 1875. 'Anandmath' was written in 1882, which is after 1875. Thus, Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay writing Anandmath happened after the establishment of Arya Samaj.

questions.question: Who was the founder of the Calcutta Madarsa, established in 1781?

answerOptions.rationale: The Calcutta Madarsa (also known as Calcutta Aliya Madrasah or Mohammadan College of Calcutta) was founded by Warren Hastings, the first Governor-General of Bengal, in 1781. The objective was to promote the study of Arabic and Persian languages and Islamic law, primarily to provide qualified Indian Muslim officers for the Company's administration of justice.

questions.question: The object of the Butler Committee of 1927 was to:

answerOptions.text: Review the working of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
Examine the relationship between the British Crown and the Indian Princely States
answerOptions.rationale: The Butler Committee, formally known as the Indian States Committee, was constituted in 1927 under the chairmanship of Harcourt Butler. Its primary objective was to investigate and clarify the relationship between the Paramount Power (British Crown) and the Indian Princely States, and to suggest measures for the more satisfactory adjustment of economic and financial relations between British India and the States. Thus, it aimed to examine and define the relationship with the Indian Princely States.

answerOptions.text: Assess the need for a separate electorate for Muslims
Formulate a new constitutional framework for India

questions.question: Who was the co-founder of the Indian Association, established in 1876, along with Surendranath Banerjee?

answerOptions.rationale: Surendranath Banerjee and Anandamohan Bose were the key founders of the Indian Association in Calcutta in 1876. This organization played a significant role in articulating Indian nationalist demands and mobilizing public opinion before the establishment of the Indian National Congress.

questions.question: The Satya Shodhak Samaj, founded by Jyotirao Phule, primarily aimed at:

answerOptions.text: Social reform and upliftment of lower castes and women
answerOptions.rationale: The Satya Shodhak Samaj (Truth-Seekers' Society), founded by Jyotirao Phule in 1873, was dedicated to social reform, particularly the upliftment of marginalized sections of society, including lower castes (Shudras and Ati-Shudras) and women. The Samaj challenged the caste system, advocated for education for all, and fought against Brahmanical dominance and exploitation.

questions.question: The Montague-Chelmsford Reforms are synonymous with which type of reforms?

answerOptions.text: Administrative reforms in the judicial system
Economic reforms related to trade and industry
Political and constitutional reforms for British India
answerOptions.rationale: The Montague-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) were fundamentally a set of political and constitutional reforms introduced by the British government for British India. They aimed to gradually introduce self-governing institutions and increase Indian participation in the administration, notably through the system of 'Dyarchy' in the provinces. They laid the groundwork for future constitutional developments.

answerOptions.text: Social reforms aimed at abolishing certain practices

questions.question: The main point of contention that led to the split of the Indian National Congress at Surat in 1907 was:

answerOptions.text: Disagreement over the leadership role of Mahatma Gandhi
Differences in approach and methods to achieve Swaraj between Moderates and Extremists
answerOptions.rationale: The Surat Split of 1907 was a culmination of widening ideological and methodological differences between the Moderates and Extremists within the Indian National Congress. Moderates advocated for constitutional methods and gradual reforms, while Extremists pushed for more assertive actions like boycotts, strikes, and Swadeshi to achieve self-rule. This fundamental disagreement over strategy and the pace of political change was the core reason for the split.

answerOptions.text: Demand for separate electorates for different religious communities

questions.question: The Cripps Mission's proposal for India's post-World War II status was:

answerOptions.text: Full independence as a sovereign republic
Integration into the British Commonwealth as a protectorate
Dominion status with the right to secede from the Commonwealth
answerOptions.rationale: The Cripps Mission in 1942 offered Dominion status to India after World War II. This implied that India would become an autonomous entity within the British Commonwealth, with the freedom to secede from it. It also proposed the formation of a Constituent Assembly, but the offer was rejected by major Indian political parties due to several reasons, including the lack of immediate transfer of power and the provision for provinces to opt out.

answerOptions.text: Limited self-government under direct British supervision

questions.question: Which prominent figure dedicated his life to the upliftment of 'Harijans' after the Poona Pact?

answerOptions.rationale: Following the Poona Pact in 1932, Mahatma Gandhi intensified his efforts for the upliftment of the untouchables, whom he termed 'Harijans' (children of God). He launched the Harijan Sevak Sangh, dedicated to removing untouchability and working for their social, economic, and political betterment, making it a central plank of his social reform agenda.

questions.question: Which of the following fruits are indigenous to the Americas (New World) and were later introduced to India by European traders?

answerOptions.rationale: Papaya, pineapple, and guava are all native to the Americas. They were introduced to India, along with many other plants like potatoes, tomatoes, and chilies, by the Portuguese explorers and traders starting from the 16th century. Mango, banana, and coconut are indigenous to the Old World (Asia and Pacific).

questions.question: The founder of the Self-Respect Movement, E. V. Ramaswamy Naicker, is famously known by which title?

answerOptions.rationale: E. V. Ramaswamy Naicker is widely known and revered in Tamil Nadu by the honorific title 'Periyar', which means 'Great Sage' or 'Elder'. He earned this title for his pioneering work in social reform, rationalism, and his efforts to promote self-respect and combat caste discrimination.

questions.question: Which Vijayanagara ruler granted permission to the Portuguese to build a fort at Bhatkal?

answerOptions.rationale: Krishnadevaraya, the illustrious ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire (1509-1529), maintained cordial relations with the Portuguese. He granted them permission to construct a fort at Bhatkal, an important port on the west coast, in exchange for their support, particularly in providing horses, which were vital for his military strength.

questions.question: The principle of 'lapse' or 'forfeiture' for failure to pay revenue on time was a characteristic feature of which land revenue system introduced by Cornwallis?

answerOptions.rationale: The Permanent Settlement, introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal in 1793, famously included a 'Sunset Clause'. Under this system, if the Zamindar (landlord) failed to pay the fixed amount of land revenue to the state by a specified date (sunset of that day), his Zamindari rights would be confiscated, and his estate would be auctioned off. This strict rule often led to the displacement of traditional Zamindars and the emergence of new landlords.

questions.question: Who presided over the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly as its provisional President?

answerOptions.rationale: Following the French practice, the oldest member present, Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, was elected as the interim or provisional President of the Constituent Assembly at its first meeting on December 9, 1946. Two days later, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent President.

questions.question: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, which subjects were retained under the direct control of the Governor-General, outside the purview of the federal legislature?

answerOptions.rationale: The Government of India Act, 1935, while proposing an All India Federation and introducing provincial autonomy, retained crucial subjects under the direct control of the Governor-General. These 'reserved' subjects included Defence, Foreign Affairs, Ecclesiastical Affairs, and Tribal Areas. The federal legislature had no control over these areas, ensuring British imperial authority remained paramount.

questions.question: Who was the Sultan of Gujarat who ceded Diu to the Portuguese in 1535?

answerOptions.rationale: Bahadur Shah, the Sultan of Gujarat, was forced to cede Diu to the Portuguese in 1535 by the Treaty of Bassein, in exchange for their military assistance against the Mughal emperor Humayun. Diu was a vital strategic port, and its acquisition marked a significant expansion of Portuguese influence in the region.

questions.question: The group of scholars and archaeologists including Alexander Rea, A. H. Longhurst, Robert Sewell, James Burgess, and Walter Elliot are primarily known for their work in:

answerOptions.text: Archaeological explorations and conservation of historical sites
answerOptions.rationale: All the mentioned individuals – Alexander Rea, A. H. Longhurst, Robert Sewell, James Burgess, and Walter Elliot – were prominent British archaeologists and historians who conducted extensive research, surveys, and excavations of ancient monuments and historical sites across India during the 19th and early 20th centuries. Their contributions were fundamental to the understanding and preservation of India's archaeological heritage.

answerOptions.text: Development of modern Indian education system

questions.question: The Governor-General of India was created for the first time by which of the following legislative acts?

answerOptions.rationale: The Charter Act of 1833 centralized British administration in India by formally creating the position of 'Governor-General of India' from the 'Governor-General of Bengal'. This made Lord William Bentinck the first holder of this new, more powerful office, overseeing all British territories in India.

answerOptions.text: The Government of India Act of 1858

questions.question: The National Handloom Day is celebrated on August 7 because it commemorates:

answerOptions.text: The establishment of the first textile mill in India
The launch of the Swadeshi Movement in 1905
answerOptions.rationale: National Handloom Day is celebrated on 7th August each year to commemorate the launch of the Swadeshi Movement on this day in 1905. The Swadeshi Movement played a crucial role in reviving indigenous industries, especially the handloom sector, by encouraging the use of Indian-made goods and boycotting foreign products. This date was chosen to honor the contributions of the handloom weaving community and to highlight the sector's importance.

answerOptions.text: The signing of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact
The adoption of the Indian Constitution

questions.question: Which of the following were 'Reserved' subjects under the Government of India Act 1919's Dyarchy system in the provinces?1. Local Self-Government2. Finance3. Agriculture4. PoliceSelect the correct code:

answerOptions.rationale: Under the Dyarchy system introduced by the Government of India Act 1919, provincial subjects were divided into 'Reserved' and 'Transferred'. Reserved subjects were administered by the Governor with his Executive Council and were not responsible to the legislative council. These included Finance (2), Police (4), Justice, Land Revenue, and Irrigation. Transferred subjects were administered by the Governor acting with ministers responsible to the legislative council, and these included Local Self-Government (1), Public Health, Education, and Agriculture (3).

questions.question: Among the given freedom fighters, who was associated with the Ghadar Party?

answerOptions.rationale: Rash Behari Bose was a prominent Indian revolutionary who, after fleeing India, became actively involved with the Ghadar Party, particularly in its activities in East Asia. He played a significant role in organizing Indian revolutionaries abroad, including efforts to orchestrate uprisings during World War I in collaboration with the Ghadarites.

questions.question: Which major proposal of the Cripps Mission (1942) granted provincial autonomy in deciding future constitutional status?

answerOptions.text: Immediate formation of a National Government
Granting universal adult franchise for constitution-making
Right for any province to opt out of the Indian Union and negotiate separately with Britain
answerOptions.rationale: A controversial but significant proposal of the Cripps Mission was that any province that was unwilling to accept the new constitution for the Indian Union would have the right to retain its existing constitutional position with Britain or to negotiate a separate agreement. This effectively conceded the possibility of India's partition, providing a degree of autonomy to provinces regarding their future political alignment.

answerOptions.text: Transfer of all defence powers to Indian hands immediately

questions.question: The capture of Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510 was a significant event for which European power?

answerOptions.rationale: Alfonso de Albuquerque, the Portuguese governor in India, captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510. This was a pivotal moment as Goa became the main trading hub and administrative center of the Portuguese Estado da India (State of India) for centuries, establishing their strong presence on the west coast of India.

questions.question: Who translated the Indian National Anthem 'Jana Gana Mana' from Bengali to English at Madanapalle?

answerOptions.rationale: Rabindranath Tagore himself translated 'Jana Gana Mana' into English at Madanapalle, Andhra Pradesh, in February 1919. He was visiting the Besant Theosophical College, and at the request of the college principal, Margaret Cousins, he undertook this translation, giving it the title 'The Morning Song of India'.

questions.question: Which of the following was a key objective behind the establishment of Fort William College in Calcutta by Lord Wellesley?

answerOptions.text: To promote Indian classical music and arts
To conduct scientific research and technological innovation
To provide training in Indian languages and administration for British civil servants
answerOptions.rationale: Lord Wellesley established Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800 with the primary goal of providing comprehensive training to British civilian recruits of the East India Company. This training included Indian languages (like Hindustani, Persian, Sanskrit), laws, history, and customs, to prepare them for administrative duties in India and ensure a more efficient and informed colonial bureaucracy.

answerOptions.text: To foster cultural exchange between Britain and India

questions.question: Who wrote the influential nationalist book ‘Desher Katha'?

answerOptions.rationale: Sakharam Ganesh Deuskar, a Marathi writer and journalist who lived and worked in Bengal, wrote the highly influential book ‘Desher Katha’ (Story of the Country) in Bengali in 1904. The book became a significant text of the Swadeshi movement, providing a sharp critique of British economic exploitation and colonial rule, inspiring many nationalists.

questions.question: Which of the following was explicitly NOT included in the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931?

answerOptions.text: Congress participation in the Round Table Conference
Withdrawal of ordinances relating to the Civil Disobedience Movement
Public inquiry into police excesses during the Civil Disobedience Movement
answerOptions.rationale: While the Gandhi-Irwin Pact included several concessions from the British side, such as the withdrawal of ordinances, the release of non-violent political prisoners, and permission to make salt for personal consumption, it explicitly did NOT include a public inquiry into police excesses. Gandhi had pressed for this, but Irwin refused, citing it would undermine the morale of the police force.

answerOptions.text: Permission for coastal residents to collect and make salt for personal use

questions.question: Who founded the All India Anti-Untouchability League in 1932?

answerOptions.rationale: Mahatma Gandhi founded the All India Anti-Untouchability League (later renamed Harijan Sevak Sangh) in 1932, shortly after the Poona Pact. This organization was dedicated to eradicating untouchability and working for the social and economic upliftment of the 'Harijans' (untouchables).

questions.question: Which of these leaders served as the President of the All India Liberal Federation?

answerOptions.rationale: Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru was a prominent Indian lawyer, politician, and statesman belonging to the Liberal faction of Indian politics. He was a leading figure in the All India Liberal Federation, serving as its President. The Liberal Federation emerged from the Moderate wing of the Congress and advocated for constitutional reforms and self-government through peaceful means.

questions.question: Which political figure was a Member of the Constituent Assembly that drafted the Indian Constitution?

answerOptions.rationale: K.C. Neogy (Kshitish Chandra Neogy) was a distinguished Indian politician who played an active role as a member of the Constituent Assembly of India, which was responsible for drafting the Constitution of India. He later served as a cabinet minister in the first government of independent India.

questions.question: P.C. Joshi was the General Secretary of which major political party in India?

answerOptions.rationale: P.C. Joshi (Puran Chand Joshi) was a prominent leader and the first General Secretary of the Communist Party of India (CPI). He played a crucial role in the early development and organization of the communist movement in India, leading the party during significant periods of its history.

questions.question: Who among the following wrote biographies of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji, and Shrikrishna, and was elected to the Central Assembly?

answerOptions.rationale: Lala Lajpat Rai, a prominent Indian nationalist and extremist leader, penned biographies of several inspiring figures including Giuseppe Mazzini and Giuseppe Garibaldi (Italian nationalists), as well as Chhatrapati Shivaji and Lord Shrikrishna. He also spent time in the United States and was later elected to the Central Legislative Assembly in British India, embodying a multifaceted role as a writer, activist, and legislator.

questions.question: The Wood's Despatch (1854) made recommendations for which of the following educational reforms?1. Establishment of a grants-in-aid system.2. Creation of universities in presidency towns.3. Exclusive use of English as the medium of instruction at all levels.Select the correct code:

answerOptions.rationale: Wood's Despatch of 1854 was a comprehensive scheme for educational reform. It recommended the establishment of a grants-in-aid system (1) to encourage private educational institutions and the establishment of universities in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras (2) on the model of the London University. However, it did not recommend the exclusive use of English at all levels (3); instead, it suggested English for higher education and vernacular languages for primary and secondary education. Thus, statements 1 and 2 are correct.

questions.question: Under the Government of India Act of 1935, to whom were the residuary powers assigned?

answerOptions.rationale: The Government of India Act of 1935 outlined a federal structure with a division of powers between the centre and provinces. However, unlike modern federations where residuary powers (powers not enumerated in any list) typically reside with the federal legislature or units, the Act vested these powers in the Governor-General. This reflected the British government's ultimate control over the Indian administration.

questions.question: Following the Santhal Uprising (1855-56), which protective measure for Santhal land was implemented by the colonial government?

answerOptions.text: Establishment of a special police force to protect Santhals
Declaration of Santhal lands as protected forests
Prohibition of land transfer from Santhals to non-Santhals
answerOptions.rationale: After the brutal suppression of the Santhal Uprising, the British government realized the need for specific measures to address tribal grievances and protect their rights. One significant step taken was the enactment of regulations that made it illegal for a Santhal to transfer land to a non-Santhal. This was aimed at preventing land alienation and safeguarding the traditional land tenure system of the Santhal community.

answerOptions.text: Introduction of a new revenue system for Santhal areas

questions.question: During the mid-18th century, which of the following was a primary export commodity for the English East India Company from Bengal?

answerOptions.rationale: In the mid-18th century, Bengal was a vital source of various goods for the English East India Company. Among the key commodities exported, saltpetre was particularly important. It was a crucial ingredient for gunpowder, making it strategically valuable for European powers involved in frequent warfare. Cotton textiles, silk, and opium were also significant exports.

questions.question: The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) marked a turning point in India's freedom struggle primarily because it:

answerOptions.text: Introduced non-violence as a novel method of protest nationwide
Saw the first active participation of industrial workers in a political movement
Successfully linked localized agrarian issues with the broader nationalist movement
answerOptions.rationale: The Champaran Satyagraha was Mahatma Gandhi's first major experiment with Satyagraha in India. Its most significant aspect was its success in bringing a local peasant issue (exploitation of indigo farmers by European planters) into the mainstream of the national freedom struggle. This demonstrated Gandhi's ability to mobilize masses around specific grievances and integrate them into the larger fight for independence, thereby broadening the base of the nationalist movement beyond urban elites.

answerOptions.text: Led to the immediate repeal of all oppressive land laws

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT an objective of the Subsidiary Alliance system, as introduced by Lord Wellesley?

answerOptions.text: To secure military assistance for British wars at the expense of Indian states
To counter the influence of other European powers, particularly France
To promote economic self-sufficiency and industrialization within allied Indian states
answerOptions.rationale: The Subsidiary Alliance system (1798) was designed by Lord Wellesley to expand British political and military control over Indian states. Its objectives included: making Indian states dependent on the British by stationing British forces in their territories (at the states' expense), curbing the influence of other European powers (like the French), and effectively bringing states under British paramountcy without direct annexation. Promoting economic self-sufficiency or industrialization in allied states was never an objective; rather, the system often led to financial strain on the states and further economic drain for India, benefiting British trade and industry.

answerOptions.text: To establish British paramountcy by controlling the foreign relations of Indian states

questions.question: The introduction of English education in India was influenced by which of these developments?1. Allocation of funds in the Charter Act of 18132. Recommendations of the General Committee of Public Instruction formed in 18233. The Anglicist-Orientalist ControversySelect the correct answer using the code given below:

answerOptions.rationale: All three factors played crucial roles in the introduction and eventual dominance of English education in India. The Charter Act of 1813 was the first instance of legislative provision for education funding. The General Committee of Public Instruction (1823) was responsible for managing these funds and debating the curriculum. The Anglicist-Orientalist Controversy, a fierce debate within this committee and broader British policy circles, ultimately led to the triumph of the Anglicists (led by Macaulay and supported by Bentinck), who advocated for English as the medium of instruction for Western knowledge, thereby laying the foundation for English education in India.

questions.question: Which of the following events occurred earliest?

answerOptions.rationale: To determine the earliest event: Dinabandhu Mitra's play 'Neeldarpan' was written in 1860. Satyendranath Tagore becoming the first Indian ICS officer was in 1863. Swami Dayanand Saraswati established the Arya Samaj in 1875. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote 'Anandmath' in 1882. Therefore, Dinabandhu Mitra writing Neeldarpan is the earliest event among the options.

answerOptions.text: Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to succeed in the Indian Civil Services Examination (1863)

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of educational institutions and their founders during colonial rule in India is/are correctly matched?1. Pair 2 is correctly matched: Calcutta Madarsa was founded by Warren Hastings in 1781 to promote the study of Islamic law and Arabic and Persian languages. Pair 3 is correctly matched: Fort William College was established by Lord Wellesley in 1800 to train British civil servants in Indian languages and administration. All three pairs are correctly matched.

questions.question: Regarding Raja Ram Mohan Roy's ideological synthesis, which statement best describes his approach toward religious scriptures?

answerOptions.text: He advocated for a total rejection of traditional Eastern philosophy in favor of Western secularism.
answerOptions.rationale: Roy actually held deep respect for the traditional philosophical systems of the East while seeking to reform them.

answerOptions.text: He sought to demonstrate that the core of Hindu scriptures was consistent with monotheism and rationalism.
answerOptions.rationale: Roy used his knowledge of the Upanishads to argue that original Hindu thought supported the worship of a single, rational deity.

answerOptions.text: He believed that scientific progress could only be achieved by converting to Christianity.
answerOptions.rationale: While influenced by Christian ethics, he sought to reform Hinduism from within using rationalist principles.

answerOptions.text: He prioritized ritualistic traditions over social equality to maintain cultural continuity.
answerOptions.rationale: He was a staunch opponent of ritualism and a champion of human dignity and social equality for both men and women.

questions.hint: Consider his work 'Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin' (A Gift to Monotheists) and his defense of the Vedanta.

questions.question: During the Non-Cooperation Movement, what was the primary purpose of establishing 'National Schools and Colleges'?

answerOptions.text: To provide technical training for the newly established indigenous heavy industries.
answerOptions.rationale: The focus was more on providing an alternative to British-controlled educational institutions rather than industrial training.

answerOptions.text: To ensure education continued for students who boycotted government-aided institutions.
answerOptions.rationale: As part of the boycott of government titles and institutions, national schools were established to provide a 'constructive' alternative.

answerOptions.text: To train a paramilitary force for a planned violent insurrection against the British.
answerOptions.rationale: The movement was strictly based on the principle of non-violence.

answerOptions.text: To implement the provisions of Wood's Despatch through private funding.
answerOptions.rationale: Wood's Despatch was a British educational policy, which the Non-Cooperation Movement sought to distance itself from.

questions.hint: Think about the 'Constructive Programme' that accompanied the boycott of British structures.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the 'Sunset Law' associated with the Permanent Settlement of 1793?

answerOptions.text: Zamindars were required to pay the revenue by sunset on a specified date or face the sale of their estate.
answerOptions.rationale: This strict provision ensured timely revenue collection but led to the downfall of many traditional landed families.

answerOptions.text: Peasants were forbidden from working in the fields after sunset to prevent the hiding of surplus grain.
answerOptions.rationale: The regulation focused on the relationship between the state and the Zamindar, not the working hours of peasants.

answerOptions.text: The British government would lower the tax rate once the sun set on the fiscal year.
answerOptions.rationale: The revenue under Permanent Settlement was fixed in perpetuity and did not fluctuate based on the time of year.

answerOptions.text: Zamindars were granted judicial powers only during daylight hours.
answerOptions.rationale: The Cornwallis Code actually stripped Zamindars of their traditional police and judicial duties.

questions.hint: This law concerned the consequences of a Zamindar's failure to meet the state's fixed revenue demand.

questions.question: In the context of the Portuguese presence in India, what was unique about the acquisition of Diu compared to earlier territories like Goa?

answerOptions.text: It was captured through a direct naval invasion against the Zamorin of Calicut.
answerOptions.rationale: Diu was part of the Kingdom of Gujarat, not the territories of the Zamorin.

answerOptions.text: It was surrendered by Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in exchange for help against the Mughal Emperor Humayun.
answerOptions.rationale: The Portuguese exploited the political pressure Bahadur Shah faced from the Mughals to secure the strategic port of Diu.

answerOptions.text: It was the first territory where the Portuguese established a factory on the East Coast.
answerOptions.rationale: Diu is located on the West Coast, and the Portuguese primarily expanded in the West first.

answerOptions.text: It was granted to them by the Gajapati rulers for the establishment of warehouses.
answerOptions.rationale: The Gajapati rulers were associated with the East Coast (Odisha), and the Dutch were more linked to them.

questions.hint: Reflect on the diplomatic maneuvers involving the Sultan of Gujarat and the Mughal threat.

questions.question: Why did the 'All India Federation' proposed in the Government of India Act, 1935, never come into existence?

answerOptions.text: The British Parliament refused to ratify the specific clause regarding the federation.
answerOptions.rationale: The clause was part of the Act passed by Parliament; the hurdle was the voluntary participation of local rulers.

answerOptions.text: The necessary number of Princely States refused to sign the Instruments of Accession.
answerOptions.rationale: The federation required a specific quota of Princely States to join voluntarily, which they failed to do.

answerOptions.text: Mahatma Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement specifically to block the federation.
answerOptions.rationale: The Quit India Movement occurred in 1942, whereas the federation plan had already stalled by the late 1930s.

answerOptions.text: The Secretary of State for India abolished the plan to focus on World War II preparations.
answerOptions.rationale: While the war delayed further constitutional talks, the failure was primarily due to the non-participation of the Princes.

questions.hint: The federation was conditional upon the voluntary joining of the Princely States.

questions.question: The 'Self-Respect Movement' led by E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker primarily targeted which of the following social structures?

answerOptions.text: The colonial educational system's focus on English language.
answerOptions.rationale: While he had views on education, his movement was primarily social and religious in nature.

answerOptions.text: Brahminical hegemony and the caste-based social hierarchy.
answerOptions.rationale: The movement sought to create a society where backward castes had equal self-respect, often through anti-Brahminical rhetoric.

answerOptions.text: The introduction of the Ryotwari system in Southern India.
answerOptions.rationale: The Ryotwari system was an economic/administrative issue, whereas Periyar's focus was socio-cultural.

answerOptions.text: The dominance of the Indian National Congress in the Quit India Movement.
answerOptions.rationale: Though he had differences with Congress, his life's mission was centered on Dravidian identity and anti-caste reform.

questions.hint: Consider the name 'Self-Respect' and the community it aimed to empower against traditional priestly dominance.

questions.question: Which specific provision regarding women was introduced by the Government of India Act, 1935?

answerOptions.text: Granting universal adult franchise to all women over the age of 21.
answerOptions.rationale: Universal adult franchise was only realized in the Constitution of independent India; the 1935 Act had limited franchise.

answerOptions.text: The reservation of seats for women in the provincial and central legislatures.
answerOptions.rationale: This Act expanded the representation of women by providing separate electorates and reserved seats.

answerOptions.text: A mandate for 50% reservation for women in all local Panchayats.
answerOptions.rationale: Reservations in Panchayats were introduced much later through the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts.

answerOptions.text: The appointment of the first female Governor in a British Indian province.
answerOptions.rationale: The Act did not mandate female governors; such appointments happened in the post-independence era.

questions.hint: Think about the expansion of representative categories in the legislature under this Act.

questions.question: Lala Lajpat Rai is noted for writing biographies of which international revolutionary figures to inspire Indian youth?

answerOptions.rationale: While he spent time in America, his primary biographical subjects for revolutionary inspiration were Italian.
The Italian unification leaders Mazzini and Garibaldi were major inspirations for the militant nationalists in India.
Lajpat Rai was more of a nationalist than a socialist revolutionary of the Leninist type.
He focused on figures whose struggles for national unification and independence mirrored the Indian context.

questions.hint: These figures were the architects of the 'Risorgimento' (Italian Unification).

questions.question: What was the critical outcome of the Butler Committee of 1927?

answerOptions.text: It recommended the immediate merger of all Princely States into British India.
answerOptions.rationale: The committee actually sought to clarify and protect the relationship between the Paramount Power and the States.

answerOptions.text: It defined the relationship between the British Paramountcy and the Indian Princely States.
answerOptions.rationale: The committee emphasized that Paramountcy must remain paramount and defined the crown's obligations toward the princes.

answerOptions.text: It established a timeline for the complete 'Indianization' of the Civil Services.
answerOptions.rationale: Civil Service reforms were handled by other bodies like the Lee Commission.

answerOptions.text: It proposed the division of subjects into 'Reserved' and 'Transferred' lists.
answerOptions.rationale: This was a feature of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Dyarchy) of 1919.

questions.hint: The committee's work was central to the grievances of the Indian Princes regarding British authority.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the introduction of crops by the Portuguese into India during the 16th and 17th centuries?

answerOptions.text: They introduced indigenous Asian crops like Sugarcane and Rice to the West Coast.
answerOptions.rationale: Sugarcane and Rice were already native to India long before the Portuguese arrived.

answerOptions.text: They brought 'New World' crops such as Pineapple, Papaya, and Cashew nuts to India.
answerOptions.rationale: The Portuguese were instrumental in the 'Columbian Exchange' that brought many American crops to the Indian subcontinent.

answerOptions.text: They were the first to cultivate Coffee and Tea on a commercial scale in the Nilgiris.
answerOptions.rationale: Tea and Coffee plantations were primarily developed by the British in the 19th century.

answerOptions.text: They introduced the cultivation of Wheat and Barley to the Deccan region.
answerOptions.rationale: Wheat and Barley had been staple crops in India since the Indus Valley Civilization.

questions.hint: Many of these fruits and nuts are now integral to Indian cuisine but originated in the Americas.

questions.question: In the Nagpur session of the Indian National Congress (1920), how did the organizational objective (creed) of the Congress change?

answerOptions.text: It shifted from 'Swaraj' to 'Purna Swaraj' (Complete Independence).
answerOptions.rationale: The demand for 'Purna Swaraj' was officially adopted later, at the Lahore session in 1929.

answerOptions.text: It changed from 'constitutional means' to 'attainment of Swaraj by all legitimate and peaceful means'.
answerOptions.rationale: This represented a shift away from purely constitutional agitation to non-violent mass action.

answerOptions.text: It declared that only armed revolution was the acceptable path to freedom.
answerOptions.rationale: Congress remained committed to non-violence (Ahimsa) under Gandhi's leadership.

answerOptions.text: It restricted membership only to those who were fluent in English to maintain administrative quality.
answerOptions.rationale: The Nagpur session actually decentralized the party and made it more accessible to the masses.

questions.hint: Consider the influence of the Non-Cooperation Movement on the party's methods of struggle.

questions.question: What was the rationale behind Wellesley establishing the Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800?

answerOptions.text: To provide a modern university education for the Indian elite in their own languages.
answerOptions.rationale: The college was intended for the training of British civil servants, not Indians.

answerOptions.text: To train young British civil servants in Indian languages and customs.
answerOptions.rationale: Wellesley believed that administrators needed to understand the local culture and languages to govern effectively.

answerOptions.text: To serve as a military academy for the newly formed Bengal Army.
answerOptions.rationale: The institution was civil in nature, focused on administrative training.

answerOptions.text: To counteract the growing influence of the French East India Company's educational missions.
answerOptions.rationale: While French rivalry existed, the primary goal was improving the quality of British administration.

questions.hint: Think about the training needs of the 'Company's writers' (civil servants).

questions.question: During the Indigo Revolt and the subsequent decline of indigo cultivation, what was the primary external factor that made natural indigo unprofitable?

answerOptions.text: The discovery of massive indigo plantations in Australia and Canada.
answerOptions.rationale: Indigo is a tropical crop; these regions were not major competitors in indigo production.

answerOptions.text: The invention of synthetic dyes in Germany at the end of the 19th century.
answerOptions.rationale: Synthetic indigo was cheaper and more consistent, leading to a collapse in demand for the natural product from India.

answerOptions.text: The British Parliament passed a law banning the import of natural indigo into the UK.
answerOptions.rationale: The British government actually protected the interests of the indigo planters as long as it was profitable.

answerOptions.text: A global blight that destroyed all indigofera plants in the Bihar region.
answerOptions.rationale: The decline was primarily economic and technological rather than a biological disaster.

questions.hint: Consider technological advancements in the chemical industry during the late 1800s.

questions.question: Who provided the legal defense for the 225 people arrested in the aftermath of the Chauri Chaura incident in the High Court?

answerOptions.rationale: While C.R. Das was a prominent lawyer, he was heavily involved in political leadership and the Swaraj Party at the time.
Malaviya's advocacy was instrumental in getting a large number of the death sentences overturned or commuted.
Motilal Nehru was a top lawyer but is not specifically credited with leading this particular defense.
Ambedkar was focusing on the rights of the depressed classes and was not the lead counsel in this nationalist-related case.

questions.hint: This individual was a four-time President of the INC and founder of Banaras Hindu University.

questions.question: Which statement regarding the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) is correct?

answerOptions.text: They introduced the system of 'Dyarchy' at the Central level of government.
answerOptions.rationale: Dyarchy was introduced at the Provincial level, not the Central level, by the 1919 Act.

answerOptions.text: They divided provincial subjects into 'Reserved' and 'Transferred' categories.
answerOptions.rationale: This system allowed partial self-government by transferring certain subjects to Indian ministers.

answerOptions.text: They granted women the right to vote in all central elections immediately.
answerOptions.rationale: The Act allowed local legislatures to decide on women's suffrage; it was not a blanket grant of the right.

answerOptions.text: They abolished the separate electorates for Muslims established in 1909.
answerOptions.rationale: The 1919 Act actually extended the principle of separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, and others.

questions.hint: Consider the concept of 'dual government' within the provinces.

questions.question: Regarding Wood's Despatch of 1854, which of the following is true?

answerOptions.text: It recommended that English be the only medium of instruction at the primary level.
answerOptions.rationale: It recommended vernacular languages for primary education and English for higher education.

answerOptions.text: It proposed a system of grants-in-aid to encourage private enterprise in education.
answerOptions.rationale: This was a key feature to expand the educational network beyond purely government-run schools.

answerOptions.text: It was primarily focused on the religious conversion of students to Christianity.
answerOptions.rationale: The Despatch emphasized secular education, though missionary schools were eligible for grants.

answerOptions.text: It discouraged the establishment of universities in presidency towns like Calcutta.
answerOptions.rationale: It explicitly recommended the establishment of universities based on the model of the University of London.

questions.hint: This document is often called the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India'.

questions.question: Who was the provisional President of the Constituent Assembly before Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected?

answerOptions.rationale: Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, not the provisional President.
Following the French practice, Sinha, as the oldest member, was elected as the temporary President on Dec 9, 1946.
Patel was a key leader but did not serve as the temporary President of the Assembly.
Rajagopalachari held many high offices but was not the temporary President of the Constituent Assembly.

questions.hint: Think of the oldest member present at the inaugural session of the Assembly.

questions.question: The 'Swadeshi Movement' (1905) had which of the following significant impacts on Indian industry?

answerOptions.text: It led to the complete nationalization of all British-owned textile mills.
answerOptions.rationale: Nationalization was not possible under colonial rule; the movement focused on boycotting British goods.

answerOptions.text: It contributed to the revival and growth of indigenous artisan crafts and industries.
answerOptions.rationale: The boycott of foreign cloth and goods created a demand that boosted local handlooms and factories.

answerOptions.text: It resulted in the British government granting immediate subsidies to Indian salt producers.
answerOptions.rationale: The British government maintained the salt tax and monopoly, which later became a focal point of the Civil Disobedience Movement.

answerOptions.text: It prevented the establishment of any new foreign-owned factories for a decade.
answerOptions.rationale: While it hurt sales of foreign goods, it did not have the legal power to stop foreign investment or factory establishment.

questions.hint: Reflect on the 'Atmashakti' (Self-Reliance) aspect of the movement.

questions.question: What was the significance of 7th August in the context of the Indian National Movement?

answerOptions.text: It marks the day Mahatma Gandhi started the Dandi March.
answerOptions.rationale: The Dandi March began on March 12, 1930.

answerOptions.text: It is the date when the Swadeshi Movement was formally launched in 1905.
answerOptions.rationale: A massive meeting at the Calcutta Town Hall on this day in 1905 marked the formal proclamation of the movement.

answerOptions.text: It is the anniversary of the signing of the Poona Pact.
answerOptions.rationale: The Poona Pact was signed in September 1932.

answerOptions.text: It marks the day the first session of the Indian National Congress was held.
answerOptions.rationale: The first session was held in late December 1885.

questions.hint: This day is now celebrated as 'National Handloom Day' to honor a specific movement.

questions.question: Which of the following were treated as 'Reserved' subjects under the system of Dyarchy introduced in 1919?

answerOptions.rationale: These were 'Transferred' subjects administered by Indian ministers.

answerOptions.text: Administration of Justice, Police, and Land Revenue.
answerOptions.rationale: These vital departments remained under the direct control of the Governor and his executive council.
These were 'Transferred' subjects intended to give Indians experience in local administration.
These were also part of the 'Transferred' list handled by elected ministers.

questions.hint: The 'Reserved' subjects were those essential for the maintenance of British authority and order.

questions.question: How did the Charter Act of 1833 change the administrative structure of British India?

answerOptions.text: It made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India.
answerOptions.rationale: This was a major step toward administrative centralization, placing all of British India under one authority.

answerOptions.text: It allowed the East India Company to retain its monopoly on the China trade for 20 more years.
answerOptions.rationale: The 1833 Act actually ended the Company's commercial activities entirely, including the China and tea trade monopolies.

answerOptions.text: It introduced a system of open competitive exams for the civil services for the first time.
answerOptions.rationale: An attempt was made in 1833, but open competition was only effectively introduced by the Charter Act of 1853.

answerOptions.text: It transferred the government of India from the Company to the British Crown.
answerOptions.rationale: This transfer occurred later, after the 1857 Revolt, through the Government of India Act 1858.

questions.hint: Think about the centralization of power in the hands of the Governor General.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'Poona Pact' of 1932?

answerOptions.text: It was an agreement between the Congress and the Muslim League on seat sharing.
answerOptions.rationale: The Lucknow Pact (1916) dealt with the Muslim League; the Poona Pact concerned the depressed classes.

answerOptions.text: It was an agreement between Gandhi and Ambedkar that provided for reserved seats for depressed classes instead of separate electorates.
answerOptions.rationale: Gandhi went on a fast against the Communal Award, leading to this compromise that preserved Hindu unity but provided political safeguards.

answerOptions.text: It mandated that only members of the depressed classes could vote in reserved constituencies.
answerOptions.rationale: The pact established joint electorates with reserved seats, meaning everyone in the constituency could vote for the candidate.

answerOptions.text: It ended the Civil Disobedience Movement and paved the way for the Second Round Table Conference.
answerOptions.rationale: This describes the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931).

questions.hint: The pact was a direct response to the British 'Communal Award'.

questions.question: In the context of land revenue systems, how did the Ryotwari settlement differ from the Permanent Settlement?

answerOptions.text: Ryotwari established the Zamindar as the sole owner of the land.
answerOptions.rationale: Permanent Settlement established Zamindars as owners; Ryotwari recognized the individual peasant (Ryot) as the owner.

answerOptions.text: Ryotwari involved a direct settlement between the state and the individual peasant.
answerOptions.rationale: The state bypassed intermediaries like Zamindars to collect revenue directly from the cultivators.

answerOptions.text: Ryotwari fixed the revenue rate in perpetuity, never to be changed.
answerOptions.rationale: The revenue under Ryotwari was subject to periodic revision (usually every 20-30 years), unlike the Permanent Settlement.

answerOptions.text: Ryotwari was primarily implemented in the Bengal and Bihar provinces.
answerOptions.rationale: Ryotwari was mainly implemented in Southern and Western India (Madras and Bombay presidencies).

questions.hint: Think about the 'intermediary' in the system.

questions.question: Which among the following was a key feature of the 'Constructive Programme' of the Non-Cooperation Movement?

answerOptions.text: The promotion of Khadi and the use of the Charkha.
answerOptions.rationale: This was intended to promote self-reliance, provide rural employment, and boycott foreign cloth.

answerOptions.text: The formation of a secret society to carry out targeted assassinations of officials.
answerOptions.rationale: Violence was strictly excluded from the movement's principles.

answerOptions.text: The encouragement of Indian youth to join the British Army for tactical training.
answerOptions.rationale: Joining the British Army would be a form of cooperation, which the movement opposed.

answerOptions.text: The immediate declaration of independent 'republics' in every village.
answerOptions.rationale: While the movement sought Swaraj, it did not involve setting up parallel sovereign republics in 1920-22.

questions.hint: Consider the symbols of economic self-reliance promoted by Gandhi.
